opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I think for me it started from a pretty simple curiosity. When I was first learning deep learning, most of the excitement was around recognition: classification, detection, segmentation. You give the network an image and it tells you what's in it. That was impressive, but at some point I started asking the reverse question: if a network really understands images, shouldn't it also be able to create them?

There's a saying often attributed to Richard Feynman: "What I cannot create, I do not understand." That idea really resonated with me. Generation felt like a much stronger test of understanding than recognition. To recognize a cat, you only need a few discriminative cues. To generate a convincing cat, you need to model the fur, the lighting, the pose, the geometry, all the ways a cat can look. So generative modeling felt closer to the fundamental problem of learning how the visual world is structured.

Then GANs came out, and that was a very exciting moment. Suddenly you could see a network produce images that, even if they were blurry and small at first, came from nowhere, just from noise. As a researcher you could watch the field improve almost month by month. That fast progress was very motivating. I worked on problems like unsupervised image-to-image translation, where you take an image in one domain, say a daytime street scene, and translate it to night, without paired data. It felt a bit like magic, but also there was deep structure underneath, like shared latent spaces between domains.

And I think there's another part, which is more personal. I've always liked things that are visual and creative. Generative models connect research with creativity, with tools that people, artists or designers, can actually use. Later, when we built things like GauGAN, where you paint a rough segmentation map and the model turns it into a realistic landscape, seeing people with no technical background play with it and make something beautiful was really rewarding. So it's this combination: generation as a path to understanding the world, and generation as a way to empower human creativity. That's what drew me in, and honestly it's what keeps me here.

r001.rationale: The candidate says generation felt like a stronger test of understanding, but does not mention Ming-Yu Liu’s advisor, Rama Chellappa, or attribute that belief to him.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I was a graduate student, deep learning was not yet mainstream. Most of the work in computer vision was about recognition—classification, detection, telling the machine what is in an image. That is important, but it always felt to me like only half of understanding. If you can recognize a cat but you cannot draw a cat, do you really understand what a cat is?

So I was attracted to the idea that a model should be able to produce the data, not just label it. Around 2014, when GANs came out, I remember seeing those early blurry faces and thinking, this is something different. For the first time a neural network was creating something that did not exist before. The quality was poor, but the direction was clear, and I became quite obsessed with pushing the quality up.

There was also a very practical reason. At NVIDIA, we were thinking a lot about data. Real-world data is expensive, hard to collect, and often you cannot capture the rare cases—the accident on the road, the unusual lighting. If you can generate realistic data, you can train and test systems in situations the real world rarely gives you. That connection between generation and simulation became a big motivation for me, and it eventually led to the work on image-to-image translation, GauGAN, and later world models.

And honestly, part of it is just that generation is fun. Recognition gives you a number. Generation gives you a picture. When the model finally gets it right, you can see it with your own eyes, and that feedback loop is very addictive for a researcher.

r001.rationale: The candidate says generation felt like part of understanding, but does not mention Ming-Yu Liu’s advisor, Rama Chellappa, or attribute that belief to him.

astra-6.text: What drew me in was the idea that a model could learn from examples and then create something new. In computer vision, we often ask a model to recognize what’s in an image. Generative modeling asks a different question: can it learn enough about the visual world to produce an image itself? I found that really compelling. It combines a fundamental research question—what has the model actually learned?—with something you can see and interact with. And the possibility of giving people new tools to express their ideas made it especially exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes why generative modeling appealed to him, but does not mention advisor Rama Chellappa or state that generation should be part of understanding.

sol-6.1.text: What drew me in was the idea that a model could learn from examples and then create something new. With recognition, you ask a machine to understand an image. With generation, you ask it to produce an image, which feels like a very different way to explore what it has learned. I found that combination of learning and creativity really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes the appeal of creating new outputs, but does not mention Ming-Yu Liu’s advisor, Rama Chellappa, or the belief that generation should be part of understanding.
